extracted.intended_audience: writers and prospective op‑ed contributors to The New York Times (opinion writers, journalists, academics, public figures)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and selection criteria used by the New York Times Opinion desk to evaluate and select submitted op-eds; covers format, editorial quality, newsworthiness, and selection filters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically 400-1,200 words; submissions of any length considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Default target is 400–1,200 words but the desk will consider pieces of any length. (Practical implication: be concise but meet the space needed to make your point.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Original (previous publication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Must not have been published anywhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Times requires original work; do not submit pieces that have appeared elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclusive to The Times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions should be sent on an exclusive basis to The New York Times Opinion desk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal insight / personal stake
rubrics_metrics.description: Author has skin in the game; personal insight is required (author's own perspective or stake).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The desk favors pieces where the author brings personal knowledge, experience, or stake that informs the argument—i.e., not purely abstract commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broader public relevance / public significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument rises beyond the personal to address public significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An op-ed should connect the author's insight or experience to matters of public interest or national conversation rather than remaining solely anecdotal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenges assumptions / provocation / counter-narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Challenges assumptions; counter-conventional wisdom; provocation that questions the status quo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The desk looks for pieces that push against received wisdom or offer a contrarian/fresh angle rather than reiterating common views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adds something new / original argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Adds something new to the national conversation; original argument, not warmed-over positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions should bring new facts, framing, or lines of reasoning that materially advance or change the conversation on a topic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific (not generic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific — not generic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vague generalities; use concrete examples, details, or precise claims that support the central thesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unique perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Author's distinct viewpoint — a unique perspective on the issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece should reflect an identifiable personal or professional angle that distinguishes it from other commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice / author's own voice / craft quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Author's own voice — not corporate-style; distinctive prose and voice/craft quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Times values a clear, individual voice and strong writing craft. Avoid passive, generic, or corporate-sounding prose; distinctive, well-crafted prose improves selection chances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness / topicality
rubrics_metrics.description: Urgent now — why this op-ed today? Tied to a peg in current news cycle or seasonally appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit why the piece matters now (a news hook, recent development, or seasonal relevance). Timeliness increases newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear thesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear thesis — the piece should have a central, readable claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State a precise central argument early and keep the piece oriented to defending or illustrating that claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise / concision
rubrics_metrics.description: Concise — focused on one idea; argued tightly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The desk prefers pieces that concentrate on a single idea and make the case succinctly rather than sprawling or diffuse essays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence-based
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence-based where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support assertions with facts, data, examples, or first‑hand knowledge when available; unsupported sweeping claims weaken credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persuasive structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Persuasive structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize the piece so that premises lead logically to the conclusion; use a compelling opening, clear progression, and effective closing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author credibility / expertise / authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Author credibility / expertise / authority — author qualified to opine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The desk considers the author's background, credentials, or relevant experience when assessing whether they are qualified to argue on the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity of viewpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: Diversity of viewpoints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection takes into account the desire to present a range of perspectives in the opinion section, so novel or underrepresented viewpoints may be favored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage gap filling / service to discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage gap filling — fills a void; service to discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pieces that address topics or angles not currently well covered by public conversation—thereby serving the discourse—are more likely to be selected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversation-starting potential
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversation-starting potential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The desk favors pieces likely to provoke reaction, discussion, or further reporting; think about the piece's potential to change or start conversations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission and response logistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Pieces can be sent through digital submission portal or to opinion@nytimes.com. Lack of response within 3 business days = pass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical submission note: send via the portal or email; if you don't receive a response within about three business days consider the piece declined.
